det_01.label: Origin: Elizabeth Hawley and the Himalayan Database
det_01.content: The Himalayan Database is a comprehensive archive of mountaineering expeditions in the Nepal Himalaya. It was built around the lifetime work of Elizabeth Hawley (1923-2018), an American journalist who moved from a research role at Fortune magazine in New York to Kathmandu in 1959 and became a Reuters correspondent in 1962. From her Kathmandu apartment she interviewed nearly every expedition entering or leaving Nepal, cross-checking summit claims with such tenacity that the climbing community nicknamed her 'the Sherlock Holmes of the mountaineering world'. In 1992 she partnered with Canadian programmer Richard Salisbury to digitize her notes. The first published edition appeared in 2004 as a CD-ROM booklet from the American Alpine Club. After Hawley's death in 2018, the non-profit organization 'The Himalayan Database' continues to maintain and freely distribute the archive (Version 2). The TidyTuesday slice released on 2025-01-21 contains two tidy tables (peaks_tidy with 480 peaks and exped_tidy filtered to expeditions with year 2020-2024) so this blog focuses on the modern, post-pandemic era of Himalayan climbing.

det_02.label: What the Nepal Himalaya actually is
det_02.content: The peaks_tidy table classifies each peak by HIMAL_FACTOR (mountain range) and REGION_FACTOR (broader region). The Nepal Himalaya is conventionally split into seven regions running west to east: Kangchenjunga-Janak, Khumbu-Rolwaling-Makalu, Langtang-Jugal, Manaslu-Ganesh, Annapurna-Damodar-Peri, Dhaulagiri-Mukut, and Kanjiroba-Far West. Within these sit the famous sub-ranges - Khumbu (which holds Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu), Annapurna, Manaslu/Mansiri, Dhaulagiri, Kangchenjunga, Makalu, plus many smaller groups. Eight of the world's fourteen 'eight-thousanders' (peaks above 8,000 m) lie wholly or partly in Nepal: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna. Heights in peaks_tidy are stored both in metres (HEIGHTM) and feet (HEIGHTF). Status is encoded in PSTATUS_FACTOR with values 'Climbed', 'Unclimbed', and 'Unknown'.

det_03.label: Spring 2023 was the deadliest Everest season ever
det_03.content: The 2020-2024 window in this dataset coincides with a structural transformation of Himalayan climbing. The 2020 season was effectively cancelled by COVID-19. Then Nepal threw the gates wide open: in spring 2023 the government issued a record 478 Everest permits, and at least 17 climbers died, making it the deadliest Everest season in history. With an average support team of 1.5 Sherpas per client, more than 1,200 people queued for the high camps that one spring. Kami Rita Sherpa pushed his personal Everest record to 28 ascents the same year. In 2024 Nepal's Supreme Court ordered limits on Everest permits, citing overcrowding. So the 2020-2024 slice captures both the pandemic shutdown and the post-pandemic boom that triggered regulatory backlash.

det_04.label: Annapurna I is the deadliest 8000er; Everest is no longer 14% lethal
det_04.content: Per the Himalayan Database itself, Annapurna I has the highest cumulative fatality-to-summit ratio of the fourteen 8000ers - 13.42% as of February 2025 (75 deaths against 559 ascents), with most deaths concentrated at a single avalanche zone around 5,900 m between Camps II and III. By contrast Everest's mortality rate, which was about 14.5% from 1922-1999, has fallen to roughly 1-3% in the 2000-2023 era thanks to obligatory oxygen, fixed-rope infrastructure, weather forecasting and helicopter rescue. The Himalayan Database is the canonical source quoted across these statistics. Within the 2020-2024 slice we should expect Annapurna and Dhaulagiri to look disproportionately dangerous, while Everest looks crowded but survivable.

det_05.label: TERMREASON, the heart of the expedition story
det_05.content: Each row in exped_tidy ends with a TERMREASON code (1-14). Codes 1-3 mean success ('Success (main peak)', 'Success (subpeak, foresummit)', 'Success (claimed)'). Codes 4-12 enumerate failure modes: 4 'Bad weather (storms, high winds)', 5 'Bad conditions (deep snow, avalanching, falling ice or rock)', 6 'Accident (death or serious injury)', 7 'Illness, AMS, exhaustion or frostbite', 8 'Lack (or loss) of supplies, support or equipment', 9 'Lack of time', 10 'Route technically too difficult, lack of experience, strength or motivation', 11 'Did not reach base camp', 12 'Did not attempt climb'. Code 13 is 'Attempt rumored' and 14 is 'Other'. This is the single richest categorical column in the dataset because it answers the dramatic question every expedition narrative ends with: did they get up, and if not, what stopped them?

det_06.label: Why supplemental oxygen matters above 8,000 m
det_06.content: Above roughly 7,500 m climbers enter the so-called 'death zone' where atmospheric oxygen is about a third of sea-level values and the human body cannot acclimatize indefinitely. Bottled oxygen lowers the effective altitude experienced by the body, dramatically improving cognition, endurance and survival odds. The exped_tidy table tracks this with a granular set of logical columns: O2USED (any bottled oxygen on the climb), O2NONE (an explicit 'no oxygen' attempt), O2CLIMB (climbing with O2), O2DESCENT (descending with O2), O2SLEEP (sleeping with O2), O2MEDICAL (used medically only), O2TAKEN (carried but not used), and O2UNKWN. Commercial Manaslu expeditions today supply roughly two bottles per member and one per Sherpa, and roughly half of clients elect to use it. Everest's mortality drop is largely attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides plus standardised rope-fixing.

det_07.label: Why this dataset matters
det_07.content: Himalayan mountaineering is one of the few extreme adventure pursuits with a near-complete public record, and that record drives concrete policy. The Himalayan Database underpins fatality statistics quoted in journalism, the rule changes Nepal's government implements, and the marketing of commercial expeditions. The 2020-2024 slice analysed here captures the moment commercialised high-altitude climbing entered its largest scale ever - and started running into crowding, regulation and rising body counts. For a general reader the data offers a rare quantitative window into a culture (Sherpa labour, summit fever, oxygen ethics) that is mostly experienced through hagiographic memoirs rather than numbers.

det_08.label: Scope suggestion for the analyst
det_08.content: Given the slice and external context, prioritise: (1) summit success vs failure breakdown by TERMREASON for 2020-2024 - the 2020 collapse, 2021 recovery, 2023 boom; (2) oxygen use vs success and oxygen vs deaths; (3) Sherpa/hired-personnel labour: TOTHIRED, SMTHIRED, HDEATHS vs MDEATHS, NOHIRED groups; (4) per-peak success and death rates focused on the eight 8000ers (compare with the 13.42% Annapurna benchmark and ~1-3% modern Everest benchmark from det_04); (5) seasonality (SEASON_FACTOR) - Spring still dominates the 8000ers; (6) nationality and host country trends (NATION, HOST_FACTOR). Caveat: the slice is filtered to 2020-2024 only, so absolute counts are modest (~880 expeditions); statistical claims about long-run history must rely on detective benchmarks, not on this slice.
